extracted.intended_audience: students and novice academic researchers learning how to craft research arguments (undergraduate/graduate students; early-career researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing, evaluating, and supporting claims in academic research reports, including choosing claim type, specifying significance, assembling reasons and evidence, and anticipating objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment and response
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge readers' questions, objections, and alternatives and respond to them; these acknowledgments relate to all parts of an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagram arguments to show acknowledgments/responses connecting to claim, reason, and evidence; state objections you expect and respond with arguments (e.g., 'I acknowledge these questions, objections, and alternatives, and I respond to them with these arguments...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Warranting the relevance of your reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: When readers may accept a reason's truth but doubt its relevance to the claim, supply a general principle (warrant) that justifies relating the particular reason to the particular claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer a generalization that links the specific circumstance to the specific consequence; include the warrant before making the inferential leap when readers might question the connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions readers must accept for a warrant to work
rubrics_metrics.description: For a warrant to justify inference, readers must accept: (1) the warrant is true; (2) the reason is true; (3) the specific circumstance in the reason plausibly instantiates the general circumstance in the warrant; (4) the specific consequence in the claim plausibly instantiates the general consequence in the warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any of these four fail, treat the warrant or its parts as subclaims that require supporting reasons and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include warrants only when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Experienced researchers state warrants only when they think readers might question the relevance of a reason to a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If readers will see the relevance, you don't need a warrant; otherwise add it—usually before making the connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build complex arguments from simple ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Support claims with two or more reasons, each supported by evidence and perhaps its own warrant; treat responses and warrants as subclaims requiring support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that each response to an objection and any disputed warrant may need its own reasons, evidence, and perhaps further warrants; include background, definitions, and explanations readers might need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thicken your argument to create ethos
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers earn reader confidence (ethos) by anticipating questions and concerns, acknowledging other views, and explaining principles of reasoning in warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project a character who considers issues from all sides and supports claims with evidence readers accept; doing so builds reputation—the tacit sixth element in every argument—answering the question 'Can I trust you?'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid falling back on what you know
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not uncritically impose familiar methods or argument types from one field onto problems in another field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn what's distinctive in your field's handling of argument elements and be flexible; seek alternative methods and multiple ways of supporting solutions rather than repeating one successful approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the kind of claim you should make (conceptual vs practical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem you pose determines the claim type: conceptual claims ask readers to understand; practical claims ask readers to act and require different supporting arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about intended action if you want readers to act; keep conceptual claims conceptual (suggest practical applications later in conclusions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub-arguments required for practical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If your claim is practical, readers will expect sub-arguments: an explanation of causes and an explanation of how your proposal will fix the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also explain why the solution is feasible (implementation), why it will cost less than the problem, why it won't create a bigger problem, and why it is cheaper/faster than alternatives; omission may lead readers to reject the whole argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate your claim: ask three questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before assembling argument, ask: (1) What kind of claim should I make? (2) Is it specific enough? (3) Will readers think it significant enough to need an argument?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to focus search for data and to decide whether the claim warrants a full argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your claim specific (specific language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific language (precise concepts and quantification) so the claim helps plan the argument and guides readers' expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include more terms in early versions; final claim should be only as specific as readers need and include only concepts developed in the argument (examples comparing vague vs. specific TV/crime claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your claim specific (specific logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be specific in the logic of a claim—elaborate it with qualifying clauses (although) or reason clauses (because) to forecast structure (acknowledgment, claim, reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an initial 'although' to acknowledge conflicting views or limits and a final 'because' to foreshadow reasons; this makes the working claim richer and easier to develop into a full argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge likely qualifications and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use introductory qualifying clauses to acknowledge (a) something readers believe but you challenge, (b) a conflicting point of view, or (c) a condition that limits scope or confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledging likely qualifications implies you understand readers' views and commits you to responding to them in the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your claim significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers judge significance by how much accepting the claim would force them to change other beliefs; significant claims change many beliefs or research practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levels of significance: new data on a common topic; using data to settle puzzles; upsetting long-settled beliefs. Gauge significance by how contestable the opposite claim is; small but useful contributions are acceptable early in a career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualify claims to enhance credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit claims to what the argument can support and modestly acknowledge limits; doing so strengthens ethos compared to arrogant certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention limiting conditions readers might plausibly think of and avoid overreaching; modest qualification builds trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limiting conditions selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Every claim has limiting conditions; mention only those conditions that readers might plausibly think of or that materially affect the claim's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists may omit obvious instrument-accuracy conditions, economists often acknowledge limits due to changing conditions; include important limits to give fuller, more accurate statements of your claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hedges to limit certainty appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualify the certainty of claims with hedges (words/phrases that limit force) to avoid appearing arrogant or smug; excessive hedging makes you seem timid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance is key: avoid absolute words (all, never, always) in many fields; watch disciplinary norms for acceptable levels of hedging. Examples: compare Crick & Watson's cautious phrasing with a more forceful version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan your argument by ordering reasons (storyboard technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order reasons to outline the logical structure of an argument; use a chart/storyboard to place claim, each reason, and supporting evidence on separate cards and test their consecutive sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read reasons across the tops of cards to see if order makes consecutive sense; move whole reason pages when reordering; focus on major reasons, not details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish evidence from reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence is a shared, public fact readers accept without question for the argument; if readers question it, it functions as a reason and needs its own evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate skeptical readers who will ask 'How do you know that?' repeatedly; provide progressively harder data (numbers, primary data, appendices) as needed to reach bedrock evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish evidence from reports of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports in your paper are representations (words, tables, graphs) of evidence; you can't include the evidence itself, only reports of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that data are constructed and shaped by collectors; the chain of reports may be several removes from the original facts—endeavor to use primary sources or get as close to them as possible and disclose how data were processed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate evidence using reliability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Test evidence for sufficiency, representativeness, accuracy/precision, and authoritative sourcing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect complete citations and bibliographies so they can check sources; if you collected data yourself, explain methods and provide raw data or appendices if skeptics might demand them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain provenance and methodology for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear how evidence was collected, by whom, and how it was processed so readers can judge its reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on secondary sources, use primary sources where possible or cite sources as close to the evidence as you can get; follow standardized methodologies of your field to encourage acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for escalating skepticism about evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect skeptical readers to ask repeated 'How do you know?' questions and be ready to provide harder evidence (raw data, questionnaires, source reliability) as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you present summary figures, be ready to show the underlying data; if using others' reports, be prepared to justify their reliability and provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make evidence acceptable by following disciplinary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence will count as such only if readers in your field accept it; following your field's standard procedures for collecting and reporting evidence increases its acceptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in sociology, do as sociologists do; when standards are followed, readers are more likely to accept your data without personally inspecting them.
